Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making eye contact with other people
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: As a bank teller, Maya had grown accustomed to the hum of daily transactions and the gentle chatter of customers. But it was precisely this ordinariness that now felt like a minefield. When a customer's voice rose in anger, even if just slightly, Maya's heart would quicken and her palms would sweat. She couldn't help but feel that she was being watched, too - as if unseen eyes were trained on her from across the room. Her colleagues' occasional attempts at playful flirting or innocent touches now made her skin crawl. These triggers brought back the memories of her torture in vivid, excruciating detail. The feeling of being bound and helpless, the sound of footsteps echoing down a corridor, the stench of disinfectant - all of it came flooding back with unsettling ease. When this happened, Maya felt overwhelmed by emotion, as if she was reliving the experience anew. She would freeze, unable to speak or move, until the memory finally receded. In an attempt to make sense of these episodes, Maya found herself overanalysing every detail - replaying conversations, scrutinizing facial expressions, and searching for hidden meanings in innocuous comments. This endless rumination only served to heighten her sense of threat, making her more jumpy and easily startled. Even the silence between transactions now seemed oppressive, as if something was waiting to pounce. As a result, Maya began to avoid eye contact with customers, fearing that their anger or frustration might spark another memory episode. She also took to compulsive spending - splurging on expensive clothes or jewelry in an attempt to distract herself from the constant feeling of being on edge. Her husband, puzzled by her sudden extravagance, couldn't understand why she felt so compelled to buy things they didn't need. The memories themselves had become a source of torment, too. Maya would wake during the night, her heart racing, and lie there listening for any sign of danger - convinced that some unseen threat lurked just beyond the shadows. Her days became a blur of avoidance and hypervigilance, as if she was forever waiting for the other shoe to drop. One evening, after a particularly grueling transaction, Maya found herself wandering aimlessly through the mall, spending money on anything that caught her eye - desperate to quiet the cacophony in her mind. It was then that she realized she needed help. The memories, triggers, and endless threat were taking their toll - eroding her relationships, compromising her work, and slowly consuming her sense of self. For Maya, seeking therapy felt like a last resort - an admission that she couldn't outrun the shadows alone. As she sat in the waiting room, clutching her purse tightly, she knew that she was about to confront the darkest corners of her own mind. What terrified her most was not the memories themselves, but the fear that she might never be able to escape their grasp - that they would forever define her as a victim, rather than a survivor.
